meta.title: Building a C compiler with a team of parallel Claudes
meta.author: mitsuhiko

comments.author: LAC-Tech
comments.text:
Who is this supposed to impress?

There are several existing, open source C compilers. LLMs are trained on open source code. How is spending 20,000 in 2 weeks to produce a worse version of things that already exist some incredible endorsement of agentic coding?

This industry sometimes, I swear...

apparently an issue with include paths which is both simple and a good example of how agentic coding can easily be fully un-aware of even the simplest issues.


So like, I'd probably consider that include path code to be just wrong in general (you'd probably want to just ask gcc where the paths are, if possible), but to be fair almost every compiler I've used that does not ship its own related standard library has had some bizarre issues finding the system includes. comments.author: amw-zero
comments.text:
Here's what was impressive for me: this was done with minimal human intervention, at a price point that is approaching the market rate for a human engineer.

Yes I know they talked about what they had to do to get this to work, it was not automatic, it's not an industrial-strength implementation, sure to all of the above. But I ask you: how much of engineering that goes on the industry is this completely fine for? I also ask you: how many teams have you been on where there was clearly much more demand for software than could be produced by the current team?

For me, on 100% of teams I've been on, the company would truly benefit from an engineering boost. There simply are not enough humans to meet that demand. If we can begin offloading more well-known tasks to agents, this seems like a big win for the industry. And then, who knows what they'll be able to do years down the line?

comments.author: Nelson69
comments.text:
It is impressive, in concept.  There are some weak parts though.  The assembler wasn’t complete and I think it might be the easiest part, the machine specification is well documented and fixed.  There isn’t nearly as much “prior art” to pull from though.  Especially 16bit real mode, it’s solved.  It’s an interesting omission, I wonder why.

I don’t know the current curriculums, but in college, in one semester, we built C-like compilers.  It was a challenge, and they weren’t great, but they built programs. They lacked some features, but the bulk of the language was there, and it was obvious how to add those features.  They certainly couldn’t build Linux, though, but there was a path to that if you were motivated and wanted to go further.  I suspect that there are hundreds or thousands of undergrad projects out there that could have been part of the source material.

There is a really wide range of quality in the world of compilers.  Building and booting the kernel is impressive, verifying that it’s correct, comparing it to what gcc builds, testing it, that stuff is hard and I suspect will reveal a lot of deficiencies.    Like all things with “AI” they seem to be both simultaneously mind blowing  and disappointing.    We need some better benchmarks for this stuff.

comments.author: refi64
comments.text:
It’s an interesting omission, I wonder why.


Probably more the code size / poor optimization issues, from the article:


While the compiler can output correct 16-bit x86 via the 66/67 opcode prefixes, the resulting compiled output is over 60kb, far exceeding the 32k code limit enforced by Linux.

comments.author: rbr
comments.text:
This was a clean-room implementation (Claude did not have internet access at any point during its development)


This is false, right? The LLM might just be regurgitating obfuscated copyrighted code. Or is "clean-room" a more loosely defined term? I thought it implies that something is made by developers who do not have previous knowledge of a certain product or domain. This allows making a strong claim (e.g. in court) that no copyright is violated. By my interpretation, Claude cannot clean-room most things by definition.

comments.author: pervognsen
comments.text:
I thought it implies that something is made by developers who do not have previous knowledge of a certain product or domain.


My understanding is that "clean room" is primarily useful for legal reasons, so whether something like this would be considered clean room is going to depend on the emerging legal precedents on LLM training and synthesis.

One methodology for clean room engineering is to have strongly separated engineering and reverse engineering teams, where the engineering team communicates in a carefully monitored and transcribed way with the reverse engineering team, as a form of legal information hygiene (with an extensive paper trail if you get sued) that prevents IP contamination in the engineering effort.

This brings up the question of whether you could use that methodology but with strongly separated teams of LLM engineering vs reverse engineering agents in order to legally IP-launder a specific project. I.e. not just making use of the information in the training set for synthesis (which the US courts seem to be ruling as fair use) but for de facto re-implementation of an existing project in a non-infringing way.

If that kind of thing starts to happen and becomes validated in the courts, my guess is that you would see a lot more software patents being filled. Which would really suck.

comments.author: Gaelan
comments.text:
One methodology for clean room engineering is to have strongly separated engineering and reverse engineering teams, where the engineering team communicates in a carefully monitored and transcribed way with the reverse engineering team, as a form of legal information hygiene (with an extensive paper trail if you get sued) that prevents IP contamination in the engineering effort.


And you insist on the engineering team consisting entirely of people who've never seen the codebase in question. Any LLM trained on the contents of GitHub has, of course, "seen" the GCC (and Clang, etc) codebase.

There are (as far as I'm aware) very much open legal questions about how much this is necessary, and to what extent someone who's previously seen a copyrighted codebase can reimplement it without infringement. There's certainly an argument that those questions apply equally to humans and LLMs. (Although I'd argue there is a material difference - humans are often able to recognize where they learned something, and make conscious effort to avoid plagiarism, whereas I'm not at all confident LLMs are capable of the same.)

But anyway: words mean things, and to me "clean room" specifically implies that the "clean" engineers have never seen the codebase you're trying to clone. This is not that.

comments.author: amw-zero

Let's take a very conservative average salary estimate for a software eng team: $50/hour. And let's say they could work 24 hours a day. 2 weeks = 336 hours = $16,800.

Multiply that by the number of people on the team, and all of a sudden this already looks like an economical approach.

2 person team: $33,600
4 person team: $67,200

Claude code team: $20,000.

comments.author: jrgtt
comments.text:
I don't want to take away the merit of this project, but isn't this heavily subject to selection bias?

They've spent $20K in two weeks, which appears to not be a lot for SF based engineers (but a far fetched reality for most), in a successful project... what about previous iterations and projects that went nowhere? What I mean here is that, it's easy to report on projects that led somewhere while excluding those that failed and haven't been reported. Is it fair to say the cost was only $20K?

By reading this report, me and my company with finite money may be allowed to dream that we can finally tackle that persky project by throwing money at the machine and expecting results like Anthropic's C compiler and Cursor's browser implementation, while the reality might be pricier and less successful, and maybe that's the point after all.


Edit: typos, typos, typos...

comments.author: a5rocks
comments.text:
I mean, I thought the "Stress testing the limits of agent teams" section was very interesting for this. The author calls out that they've tried this(?) on earlier models as a standard benchmark:


Previous Opus 4 models were barely capable of producing a functional compiler. Opus 4.5 was the first to cross a threshold that allowed it to produce a functional compiler which could pass large test suites, but it was still incapable of compiling any real large projects. My goal with Opus 4.6 was to again test the limits.


and then also there's an interesting bulleted list of things that Opus 4.6 didn't do (no 16-bit x86 compiler, no assembler, no linker, poor optimizer, meh code).

I think that there's some level of selection bias and the author is incentivized here to make people try the newest models, it's hard to think of a way to avoid this? Like, any blog post they post will be subject to this. I guess Anthropic (or whoever wants to convince others) should preregister any experiments like this? Given that these articles are tied to model releases, that might not be possible... but would be very nice.

comments.author: pja
comments.text:
This is simultaneously deeply impressive & completely useless in the real world. It’s an AI Rorschach test for developers!

It compiles the Linux kernel a a bunch of other OSS projects (amazing!). But it only compiles one specific version of the Linux kernel. Suspicious. Exactly how brittle is this compiler? Very, by the looks of things.

The type checker apparently doesn’t do type checking, so it will happily accept type incorrect programs & spit out code that does ... something. If it gets that far.

& the only way to even get this far was to use an existing C compiler as a test harness.

It’s a $20,000 inference (plus developer time costs that probably exceed that) art project. I love it. Give me more!

comments.author: gcupc
comments.text: Apparently, at release, it could compile (one specific version of) the Linux kernel, but it couldn't compile Hello World. So there surely must be some over-fitting to the problem space and tests.

comments.author: pja
comments.text:
The reason it can’t compile Hello World otb is because it doesn’t know where the system headers are - which is pretty typical for any compiler you install outside the standard OS packaging system.

This compiler has plenty of flaws but an inability to compile Hello World is not actually one of them - it just needs the appropriate -I include arguments
